brief.title: 300 Years of Sclerosponge Thermometry Shows Global Warming Has Exceeded 1.5 °C
brief.one_liner: Sclerosponge-derived ocean temperature records spanning three centuries reveal that anthropogenic warming has already surpassed the critical 1.5 °C Paris Agreement threshold when measured against a true pre-industrial baseline.
brief.goal: Convey to the scientific community that conventional instrumental records underestimate total warming because they start too late, and that sclerosponge proxies push the estimated warming ~0.5 °C higher, meaning 1.5 °C has already been exceeded.

sections.title: Why Sclerosponges?
sections.objective: Explain the proxy method: sclerosponges incorporate Sr/Ca ratios that track sea-surface temperature, providing continuous records back to ~1700 CE — well before instrumental coverage.

sections.title: Pre-Industrial Baseline Matters
sections.objective: Show that the IPCC's 1850–1900 reference period already contained ~0.5 °C of anthropogenic warming, so total warming from a true pre-industrial baseline is substantially higher than commonly reported.

sections.title: 300-Year Temperature Reconstruction
sections.objective: Present the reconstructed temperature anomaly timeline from ~1700 to present, highlighting the inflection points and the crossing of the 1.5 °C threshold.

sections.title: Policy & Climate Target Implications
sections.objective: Discuss what exceeding 1.5 °C means for Paris Agreement targets, remaining carbon budgets, and the urgency of mitigation action.

sections.title: Data & Methods
sections.objective: Briefly summarize sclerosponge sampling locations, Sr/Ca calibration, and comparison with HadCRUT5 and other instrumental datasets.
